title: Demand rises
contexts: Flats within 0.2 miles of a London tube station rent for considerably more than flats more than 0.5 miles away. Explain why using supply and demand.
Japanese TV dramas and cartoons became hugely popular, and many more people now want to visit Japan. Analyse the effect on the market for holidays to Japan.
A rise in consumer incomes increases the demand for a normal good such as restaurant meals. Analyse the effect on the market.
A heatwave sends temperatures to record highs. Analyse the effect on the market for ice cream.
The price of petrol rises sharply, so more people switch to electric cars. Analyse the effect on the market for electric cars.
A celebrity influencer starts wearing a particular brand of trainers. Analyse the effect on the market for the trainers.
Incomes rise in a growing economy. Analyse the effect on the market for foreign holidays.
A new university opens in a town. Analyse the effect on the market for rented student flats.
what: A shift of the demand curve to the right, caused by a non-price factor. Price and quantity both rise.
eval: Ceteris paribus rarely holds: other things change at the same time and can offset the shift.
The size of the shift matters: a 2% rise in demand and a 200% rise have very different effects.

title: Demand falls
contexts: During lockdown there was a monumental fall in the price of petrol across the UK. Explain why, using supply and demand.
A fall in incomes in a downturn reduces demand for a luxury good. Analyse the effect on its price and quantity.
Better alternatives mean consumers have stopped demanding DVD players. Analyse the effect on the market.
The price of a close substitute for a soft drink falls. Analyse the effect on the market for the soft drink.
Incomes fall in a recession. Analyse the effect on the market for restaurant meals.
A health scare about sugar changes tastes. Analyse the effect on the market for sugary drinks.
Streaming services replace rented films. Analyse the effect on the market for film rental shops.
Cold weather arrives early. Analyse the effect on the market for ice cream.
what: A shift of the demand curve to the left. Price and quantity both fall.
eval: If supply is highly elastic, the price barely falls and the quantity bears the change.
Consumers may have stocked up earlier, so the fall in demand shows up with a lag.

title: Supply rises (costs fall)
contexts: New grass strains let Brazilian ranches feed more cattle per hectare. Analyse the effect on the market for beef.
Technology reduces the plastic needed per water bottle. Analyse the effect on the market for bottled water.
Over time a calculator has fallen from £100 in 1975 to about £5 today. Explain this using supply and demand.
A new factory in a low-wage country cuts the cost of making clothes. Analyse the effect on the market for clothing.
Improved farming technology raises wheat yields. Analyse the effect on the market for wheat.
Two Asian airlines enter the London to New York market. Analyse the effect on the market for flights.
A council relaxes planning rules for new flats to rent. Analyse the effect on the market for rented flats.
The government releases surplus public land to developers. Analyse the effect on the market for new housing.
what: A shift of the supply curve to the right. The price falls and the quantity rises.
eval: In an imperfectly competitive market firms may not pass the saving on, so the price may not fall much.
It depends on the size of the cost fall and on elasticity of demand.

title: Supply falls (costs rise)
contexts: Extreme weather cuts the Dutch carrot harvest by 46%. Analyse the effect on the market for carrots.
The pound falls 10% against the euro and UK car manufacturers import rubber and glass from Western Europe. Analyse the effect on the market for UK cars.
The world price of yeast rises. Analyse the effect on the market for white bread.
Floods destroy cotton crops across Asia. Analyse the effect on the market for clothing.
Tighter environmental rules restrict where oil can be drilled. Analyse the effect on the market for oil.
Falling productivity among cocoa farmers raises their costs. Analyse the effect on the market for chocolate.
A 10% tax is introduced on high-fat frozen foods such as pizza. Analyse the effect on the market for frozen pizza.
Wages rise for staff in a hotel chain. Analyse the effect on the market for hotel rooms.
what: A shift of the supply curve to the left. The price rises and the quantity falls.
eval: Whether ceteris paribus holds: weak demand at the same time could push the price down instead.
The size of the change: a 0.5% fall in sterling hardly moves the equilibrium, a 10% fall moves it a lot.

title: Demand rises, supply fixed
contexts: Before the 2016 Olympic 100m final, reports suggested fans would pay up to £2,000 for a ticket with a face value of £90. Explain this using a supply and demand diagram.
A stadium sells out for a cup final and tickets are resold at many times face value. Explain the resale price.
A famous band announces one final concert in a 20,000-seat arena. Analyse the effect on ticket prices.
A limited edition trainer is released in a fixed number of pairs and demand surges. Explain the resale price.
Hype builds around a heavyweight title fight in a sold-out venue. Explain why prices on the resale market rise.
what: With supply fixed, a rise in demand changes only the price. This is perfectly inelastic supply in action.
eval: In the long run supply is less fixed: bigger venues or more matches can be arranged.
Face-value rules or touting laws can stop the price reaching the equilibrium level.

title: Demand falls, supply fixed
contexts: At the Rio Olympics, archery tickets with a face value of £80 were reported on sale for as little as £20 on the day. Explain using supply and demand.
A concert venue is half empty at the advertised price and sells the remaining seats cheaply on the night. Explain this.
A football match is played on a rainy weekday with a weak fixture. Explain why tickets are sold cheaply on the day.
A theatre cannot fill its seats for a poorly reviewed show. Explain the last-minute price cuts.
what: With supply fixed and demand weak, the price must fall to clear the market, because unsold seats earn nothing once the event starts.
eval: Organisers can cut supply in advance with smaller venues, or sell more cheaply earlier.
Cheap resale may also reflect sellers desperate to sell, not a true equilibrium.

title: Economic growth: outward shift
contexts: A rise in the quantity and quality of factors of production increases an economy's productive capacity. Show this on a PPF.
Improved education and technology raise productivity across the economy. Show the effect on its PPF.
A country invests heavily in capital goods and in training for its workforce. Show the long-run effect on its PPF.
A rise in net migration expands the labour force. Show the effect on potential output.
The discovery of large reserves of a natural resource increases a country's factors of production. Show the effect on its PPF.
what: An outward shift of the PPF means a rise in potential output, which is long-run economic growth.
eval: A shift shows only potential output: the economy may not move to the new frontier.
Growth may use up resources or hurt the environment, so it may not be sustainable.

title: War or disaster: inward shift
contexts: A war destroys factories, homes and infrastructure. Show the likely impact on an economy's PPF.
A severe flood destroys farmland and machinery. Show the effect on potential output.
A volcanic eruption destroys farmland and roads. Show the effect on the economy's PPF.
A long civil war emigrates a large part of the skilled workforce. Show the effect on potential output.
what: An inward shift of the PPF: a fall in productive capacity, so less of both goods can be produced.
eval: The loss may not be permanent: reconstruction and investment can rebuild capacity.
Some sectors may be hit far more than others, so the frontier may not shrink equally.

title: Technology in one good: pivot
contexts: A new production technology raises the output of consumer goods but not capital goods. Show the effect on the PPF.
Automation lifts productivity in consumer-goods factories only. Show the effect on potential output.
A breakthrough in farming technology raises food output but does not affect machinery. Show the effect on the PPF.
Improved training in the services sector raises services output only. Show the effect on the PPF.
what: A pivot of the PPF: potential output rises for one good only.
eval: Society only benefits if it actually wants more of the good that got cheaper to produce.
Resources may be slow to move between sectors, so the gain takes time.

title: Opportunity cost along the PPF
contexts: A government has a limited budget and many competing uses. Use a PPF to show the opportunity cost of spending more on capital goods.
Explain, using a PPF, why choosing more of one good always means giving up some of another.
A government decides to spend more on defence and less on health with a fixed budget. Use a PPF to show the opportunity cost.
A farmer can use the same land for wheat or for barley. Use a PPF to show the opportunity cost of growing more wheat.
A household decides how to use limited income between two goods. Show the idea of scarcity and choice with a PPF.
what: Scarcity forces choice. A movement along the PPF shows the opportunity cost: the next best alternative given up.
eval: The PPF is drawn concave because resources are not equally good at making both goods.
Opportunity cost is hard to measure when goods are not directly comparable.

title: An indirect tax
contexts: A government imposes a tax on a good. Using a diagram, show the effect on price and quantity and shade the revenue raised.
A tax on airlines is introduced to reduce a negative externality of production. Use a diagram to show the effect on price and output.
Cigarettes are taxed to reduce consumption. Show who bears the burden of the tax and the revenue raised.
A sugar tax is placed on soft drinks. Use a diagram to show the effect on price and quantity and shade the tax revenue.
The government raises the duty on fuel. Show the burden on consumers and producers and the revenue raised.
A tax is placed on plastic bags. Analyse the effect on the market for plastic bags.
what: A tax shifts supply to the left by the amount of the tax per unit. Price rises from P₁ to Pc and quantity falls. The burden is shared between consumers and producers.
eval: If demand is inelastic, the tax raises revenue but changes behaviour very little.
It is hard to set the tax equal to the external cost, and it may be regressive.

title: A tax with inelastic demand
contexts: Tax on cigarettes: smokers are addicted, so demand is inelastic. Show using a diagram why the tax raises revenue but changes consumption little.
A tax is placed on alcohol, for which demand is price inelastic. Show why the quantity falls only slightly.
A tax on petrol raises large revenue but changes driving little. Use a diagram to explain this.
what: With inelastic demand the consumption barely falls. The tax raises a lot of revenue but does little to cut the harm.
eval: Information campaigns may work better when consumers are not price sensitive.
The tax may be regressive, since poorer households spend more of their income on these goods.

title: A subsidy
contexts: The government subsidises local bus and train services. Show the effect on price and quantity and the cost to the government.
A subsidy is given to encourage the consumption of a good with a positive externality, such as education. Illustrate the effect.
The government subsidises solar panels. Show the effect on price and quantity and the cost to the government.
A subsidy is given for childcare to help parents return to work. Use a diagram to show the effect.
The government subsidises affordable housing. Analyse the effect on the market.
what: A subsidy shifts supply to the right by the subsidy per unit. Price falls, quantity rises, and both consumers and producers gain.
eval: It is expensive and may need to be paid for through higher taxes: an opportunity cost.
Producers may keep the subsidy as profit, and if demand is inelastic quantity barely rises.

title: Negative externality of production
contexts: Flights from London to New York cause global warming that airlines do not pay for. Explain, using a diagram, why the market fails.
A factory pollutes a river and imposes clean-up and health costs on others. Use a diagram to show the welfare loss.
A coal power station emits carbon dioxide that damages the climate. Use a diagram to show the market failure.
A chemical plant dumps waste into the air, land and water around it. Use a diagram to show the welfare loss.
A budget airline makes cheap flights but ignores the cost of emissions. Explain the market failure with a diagram.
what: MSC = MPC + external cost. The market produces at Qm where MPB = MPC, more than the socially optimum Q* where MSB = MSC.
eval: Valuing the external cost in money is very hard, so Q* is uncertain.
If the cost is small, the welfare loss may be less than the cost of intervening.

title: Positive externality of consumption
contexts: Education raises earnings for the individual and also raises productivity and tax revenue for everyone. Explain why it is under-consumed using a diagram.
Immunisation of children protects the child and people who are not immunised. Use a diagram to show the market failure.
List the private and external benefits of swimming and show on a diagram why it may be under-consumed.
Vaccination reduces the spread of disease to people who are not vaccinated. Show why it is under-consumed.
Training workers raises their productivity and the wages other firms can pay. Use a diagram to show the market failure.
Getting a flu jab benefits the individual and everyone they come into contact with. Explain with a diagram.
what: MSB = MPB + external benefit. The free market stops at Qm; society would want Q*.
eval: External benefits are as hard to value as external costs.
Some claimed external benefits are really private benefits the individual captures.

title: Negative externality of consumption
contexts: Smoking in public places harms others through passive smoking, smell and litter. Use a diagram to show the market failure.
Cigarettes give private benefits but impose costs on third parties. Explain why they are over-consumed.
Drinking alcohol can lead to antisocial behaviour and costs for the NHS. Use a diagram to show the market failure.
Eating fast food regularly raises health costs borne by others. Use a diagram to show the over-consumption.
what: MSB lies below MPB. Individuals ignore the cost to third parties, so there is over-consumption.
eval: If demand is inelastic, a tax barely cuts consumption.
Information may already be widely known; the issue may be addiction rather than ignorance.

title: Positive externality of production
contexts: A firm invests heavily in R&D to make production greener, and others can use the breakthrough. Use a diagram to show the market failure.
A new housing estate creates jobs, new businesses and higher house prices around it. Show the externality using a diagram.
A company develops a new battery technology that other firms can copy. Use a diagram to show the market failure.
A bee farmer's hives pollinate the orchards next door. Use a diagram to show the market failure.
what: MSC lies below MPC. The firm ignores the reduced costs to third parties, so there is under-production.
eval: The spillover is hard to value, so the correct subsidy is uncertain.
Patents and first-mover advantages can return some of the benefit to the firm.

title: A maximum price (price ceiling)
contexts: The government introduces rent controls to make housing more affordable. Use a diagram to show the effect.
A price cap is placed on energy. Show using a diagram why a shortage and a black market may result.
A city introduces a maximum rent on flats to help low-income tenants. Show the effect on the rental market.
A government caps the price of a basic food during a shortage. Show the effect on the market.
A maximum price is set on concert tickets. Use a diagram to show why a black market may develop.
what: A maximum price is set below the equilibrium. Excess demand (a shortage) results, so the good must be rationed in some other way.
eval: Rent controls can make housing more affordable but ultimately worsen the shortage.
A black market is highly likely, so some consumers may pay more than before.

title: A minimum price (price floor)
contexts: Minimum unit pricing is introduced for alcohol. Use a diagram to show the effect and the surplus created.
Governments set a minimum price to support farmers' incomes. Illustrate the effect on the market.
A government sets a minimum price for milk to support dairy farmers. Show the effect and the surplus.
A minimum price per unit of alcohol is introduced to reduce harmful drinking. Use a diagram to show the effect.
what: A minimum price is set above the equilibrium. Excess supply (a surplus) results and consumers pay more.
eval: If demand is inelastic (addictive goods) the policy may be ineffective at cutting consumption.
Where to set it: too high and surpluses and black markets grow.

title: Aggregate demand rises
contexts: Interest rates fall and consumer confidence rises. Using an AD/AS diagram, analyse the effect on real GDP and the price level.
The government increases spending when the economy has spare capacity. Use a diagram to show the likely effect.
The Bank of England cuts interest rates in a recession. Use an AD/AS diagram to show the likely effect.
A rise in house prices boosts consumer confidence and spending. Use a diagram to show the effect on real GDP.
Government investment in infrastructure increases AD when there is spare capacity. Use a diagram to show the effect.
what: An increase in any component of AD (C, I, G or X - M) shifts the curve right. The effect on output against prices depends on spare capacity.
eval: The closer the economy is to full capacity, the more the effect is on prices rather than output.
The size of the shift depends on the multiplier, which depends on leakages.

title: Demand-pull inflation near capacity
contexts: A boom in consumption pushes AD up when the economy is close to full capacity. Analyse the effect on the price level.
The economy is near full capacity and the government cuts taxes. Use a diagram to show the effect on inflation.
A surge in export demand hits an economy with very little spare capacity. Show the effect on the price level.
what: Near the productive capacity of the economy, extra demand is met mainly by higher prices.
eval: A weaker exchange rate or import prices may add to inflation at the same time.
It may be temporary if supply responds in the long run.

title: Aggregate demand falls
contexts: A fall in consumer confidence and investment leads to a recession. Use an AD/AS diagram to show the effect on real GDP.
The government cuts public spending sharply during a downturn. Use an AD/AS diagram to show the effect.
A financial crisis hits business confidence and investment falls. Show the effect on real GDP.
what: A fall in AD cuts real GDP. Output falls below capacity, so a negative output gap opens.
eval: Wages and prices may be sticky, so the adjustment is slow.
Automatic stabilisers and policy may soften the fall.

title: Cost-push: AS shifts left
contexts: A sharp rise in global energy prices raises production costs across the economy. Use an AD/AS diagram to analyse the effect.
A sudden rise in wages and import prices hits firms. Show the effect on the price level and output.
A rise in the national minimum wage raises costs across many firms. Use a diagram to show the effect.
The pound falls sharply, raising the cost of imported raw materials. Use an AD/AS diagram to show the effect.
what: A decrease in aggregate supply: prices rise and output falls together.
eval: The size of the rise in costs and how much firms pass on.
It may be temporary if costs reverse.

title: Supply-side improvement: AS shifts right
contexts: A government invests in education and infrastructure to raise productivity. Use an AD/AS diagram to show the effect.
Technology and training raise labour productivity across the economy. Show the effect on growth and prices.
The government cuts corporation tax and deregulates to encourage investment. Use a diagram to show the effect.
A programme of apprenticeships raises the skills of the workforce. Use a diagram to show the effect on the economy.
what: An increase in aggregate supply: higher output with lower inflationary pressure.
eval: Supply-side policies are slow, costly and uncertain in their effect.
The gains may be unevenly shared.

title: The multiplier
contexts: The government increases spending by £2bn and national income rises by more. Use a diagram to explain the multiplier effect.
A rise in investment sets off rounds of extra spending. Explain, with a diagram, why the total effect on GDP is larger.
A rise in business investment of £1bn leads to a larger rise in national income. Use a diagram to explain this.
The government builds a high-speed railway, and local spending rises in several rounds. Explain with a diagram.
what: The multiplier is the ratio of the final change in national income to the initial injection. 1 divided by (1 minus MPC), or 1 over the marginal propensity to withdraw.
eval: Near full capacity much of the effect is on prices, not output.
Crowding out and time lags can reduce the size of the effect.

title: AD rises above full employment
contexts: A rise in consumer spending pushes AD above the full-employment level. Using an AD/SRAS/LRAS diagram, explain the short-run and long-run effects.
A boom raises AD above full employment in the short run. Use an AD/SRAS/LRAS diagram to explain what happens as wages adjust.
Consumer confidence surges and unemployment falls below its natural rate. Use a diagram to show the long-run outcome.
what: In the neo-classical view the LRAS is vertical at the full-employment level, so demand-side policy only changes the price level in the long run.
eval: Keynesians argue the economy can be stuck below full employment for a long time, so the long-run adjustment may be slow.
The speed of adjustment depends on how flexible wages and prices are.

title: Supply-side growth: LRAS shifts right
contexts: Investment in education and technology increases the productive capacity of the economy. Use an AD/AS diagram to show the long-run effect.
A government increases spending on education and R&D. Use a diagram to show the long-run effect on potential output.
A new technology raises productivity across the economy. Use a diagram to show the effect on LRAS.
what: A shift of LRAS to the right is an increase in potential output: sustainable growth without extra inflation.
eval: The shift only shows potential: AD must be high enough for the economy to use it.
Supply-side effects take years and are uncertain.

title: Profit maximisation
contexts: A firm is the only supplier of a product and maximises profit. Use a diagram to show its price, output and supernormal profit.
A natural monopolist faces high fixed costs and falling average costs. Show the profit-maximising position.
A pharmaceutical company holds a patent on a new drug. Use a diagram to show its profit-maximising price and output.
A water company is the only supplier in its region. Use a diagram to show its supernormal profit.
what: The firm produces where MR = MC, then reads the price off AR (demand). Profit is the gap between AR and AC, times output.
eval: Contestability: the threat of entry may force the firm to price lower.
Dynamic efficiency: supernormal profit may fund innovation.

title: Costs rise
contexts: A monopolist's variable costs of production rise. Show the effect on its price, output and profit.
A monopolist faces higher energy bills. Use a diagram to show the effect on its price and output.
A single supplier of a service sees wages rise. Show the effect on its profit-maximising position.
what: A rise in variable costs shifts MC and AC up, cutting the profit-maximising output and raising the price.
eval: How much of the cost rise is passed on depends on elasticity of demand.
A monopolist with market power may absorb some costs in profit.

title: Demand rises
contexts: Demand for a monopolist's product rises. Show the effect on price, output and supernormal profit.
A successful advertising campaign increases demand for a monopolist's product. Show the effect on price and profit.
A rise in incomes increases demand for a luxury good supplied by one firm. Show the effect on output and price.
what: A rise in demand shifts AR and MR right, raising output, price and profit.
eval: Barriers to entry decide whether the higher profit lasts.
Higher profit may attract regulators or new entrants.

title: Supernormal profit then entry
contexts: In a perfectly competitive market a firm makes supernormal profit in the short run. Use a diagram to explain what happens in the long run.
Farmers growing a standard crop in a competitive market earn supernormal profit because the price is high. Explain the long run.
A fashionable new market has low barriers to entry and high profits. Use a diagram to show what happens over time.
what: No barriers to entry: supernormal profit is competed away. The firm ends allocatively and productively efficient at the minimum of AC.
eval: Few real markets are perfectly competitive.
Dynamic efficiency suffers because there is no profit to fund R&D.

title: Losses then exit
contexts: In a perfectly competitive market firms are making a loss. Use a diagram to show what happens in the long run.
A glut of a standard product pushes the price below average cost for all firms. Show what happens over time.
Falling demand leaves firms in a competitive industry making losses. Use a diagram to explain the long run.
what: Firms leave until the price returns to the minimum of AC. Losses cannot last in the long run.
eval: Firms may stay in the short run if the price covers average variable cost.
Exit can take time when capital is specialised.

title: Appreciation of the pound
contexts: Higher UK interest rates attract foreign investors. Use a diagram to show the effect on the value of the pound.
Foreign demand for UK exports rises. Show the effect on the exchange rate.
Foreign investors buy UK shares and property in large amounts. Use a diagram to show the effect on the pound.
The Bank of England raises interest rates above those abroad. Use a diagram to show the effect on sterling.
what: A rise in demand for the currency raises its value against others: an appreciation.
eval: The effect on the trade balance depends on elasticities (Marshall-Lerner) and the J-curve timing.
Central bank intervention may offset the move.

title: Depreciation of the pound
contexts: UK interest rates fall relative to the rest of the world. Show the effect on the value of the pound.
The pound is expected to fall 10% against the euro. Use a diagram to show the effect on the exchange rate.
Confidence in the UK economy falls and investors sell pounds. Use a diagram to show the effect on sterling.
The Bank of England cuts interest rates sharply. Use a diagram to show the likely effect on the pound.
what: A fall in the value of the currency. Exports cheaper abroad, imports dearer at home, with a likely rise in import costs for firms.
eval: Higher import costs may feed inflation.
A depreciation may not improve the trade balance in the short run because of the J-curve.

title: A tariff
contexts: The UK imposes a tariff on imports of steel. Use a diagram to show the effect on domestic output, imports and government revenue.
A government uses a tariff to protect an infant industry. Illustrate the effect on the market.
The government imposes a tariff on imported cars to protect domestic producers. Use a diagram to show the effect.
A country places a tariff on imported food. Show the effect on domestic output, imports and revenue.
what: A tariff is a tax on imports. Imports fall, domestic output rises, domestic consumers pay more, and the government collects revenue.
eval: Retaliation by trading partners can leave everyone worse off.
Protection can reduce incentives for domestic firms to become efficient.
